clue.text: Second overdose in vein

parts.note: a mo is a moment, a brief second of time

explanation.surface: A drug user injects a second overdose into a vein.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vein' is not a blood vessel here but a manner or tone, as in 'in a playful vein'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe a prevailing temper or tone of feeling, as in a humorous vein or a humorous frame of mind.

clue.text: I'm in Paris, nearly — time to find religious chap

indicators.note: nearly means the French phrase stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: the French for 'I am' is je suis

explanation.surface: A traveller in Paris, almost out of time, seeks a churchman.
explanation.definitionFit: A Jesuit is a member of the Society of Jesus, a Roman Catholic order of priests, so a religious man.

clue.text: Recollected no blame's attached to new duke?

indicators.note: attached to says the next piece is joined on after the anagram
recollected read as re-collected, gathered up again in a new order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone remembers that no blame was pinned on a newly made duke.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'blame's' is part of the fodder phrase only as 'no blame'; the question mark marks the definition as an example, a duke being one kind of peer.
explanation.definitionFit: A duke is the highest rank of British peer, an example of a titled aristocrat.

clue.text: Some aphrodisiac! A journo gives you wood

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A cheeky boast that a journalist's aphrodisiac gives a man an erection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives you wood' has a smutty slang reading; here it simply means 'is a type of timber'.
explanation.definitionFit: Acajou is a name for mahogany and for the cashew tree, both sources of timber.

clue.text: Follows fashion (does funny man do well?)

parts.note: the question 'does X do well?' is recast as 'is X a hit?', so does stands for is
a wit is a clever, funny person
to do well is to be a hit

explanation.surface: A comedian wonders whether keeping up with trends will help his act succeed.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as the question 'is wit hit?', meaning 'does the funny man do well?'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is with it is up to date and fashionable, keeping in step with current trends.

clue.text: Host service for flying doctors centrally

parts.note: the RAF, the Royal Air Force, is the British armed service that flies

indicators.note: centrally says to take the middle letter of the word doctors

explanation.surface: The air force provides a service flying doctors to remote places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Host' is not someone entertaining guests but a large number, as in 'a host of problems'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean a large number or great quantity, as in a raft of new measures.

clue.text: Total space traveller's taking over

parts.note: a comet is a body travelling through space
O is the cricket abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: A space traveller takes command of the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to total is to amount to, as in 'the bill comes to ten pounds'.

clue.text: Musician surprises with short cover

parts.note: to rock someone is to shock or surprise them

indicators.note: short says the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a tarp, short for tarpaulin, is a waterproof cover

explanation.surface: A musician springs surprises with a brief cover version.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover' suggests a cover version of a song, but it is a sheet of canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: A rock star is a famous performer of rock music, so a celebrated kind of musician.

clue.text: Rogue artist's balance in detail

parts.note: RA, a Royal Academician, is the usual crossword artist

indicators.note: read as de-tail, removing the tail, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a scale is a balance for weighing

explanation.surface: A painter's rogue work shows balance in its fine detail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in detail' looks like 'thoroughly' but is read as de-tail, docking the end of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Rogue and rascal are synonyms for a mischievous, dishonest person.

clue.text: Man's place also dug up

indicators.note: up here means disturbed or out of place, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man's garden has also been dug up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is not a person but the Isle of Man, a self-governing island in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas is the capital town of the Isle of Man, so a place belonging to that island.

clue.text: They support one's bits, boxing

indicators.note: boxing means the bits enclose the next piece as a box would

parts.note: jots are tiny bits, as in 'not a jot'
one is I and the 's is S, together IS

explanation.surface: Something supports a boxer's body parts, a nod to a protective box.
explanation.definitionFit: Joists are the horizontal beams that hold up a floor or ceiling, so things that bear weight.

clue.text: Small church pot makes you silent

parts.note: a pot belly is a big tum, so pot means tummy

explanation.surface: A vessel in a little church strikes visitors dumb.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping schtum is an informal phrase, from Yiddish, for keeping quiet and saying nothing.

clue.text: Origin of complaint one can lodge

indicators.note: origin of points to the first letter of complaint, where the word begins

parts.note: a means one, as in 'a pound'
a bin is a can for rubbish, as in a trash can

explanation.surface: Someone with a grievance can lodge a complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lodge' looks like a verb, to lodge a complaint, but it is the noun for a small hut.
explanation.definitionFit: A lodge and a cabin are both small, simple wooden houses, often in the countryside.

clue.text: A druggie's problem, short of capital

indicators.note: short of says the phrase is cut by its final letter

parts.note: a bud habit, bud being slang for cannabis, is a drug user's problem

explanation.surface: A drug addict's trouble is being short of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' tempts as money, the thing the addict lacks, but it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Abu Dhabi is the capital city of the United Arab Emirates.

clue.text: Head back to lab immediately

indicators.note: back to points to the final letter of lab, its back end

parts.note: once can mean as soon as, as in 'once he arrived, we left'

explanation.surface: A scientist is told to head back to the lab straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: BONCE is British slang for the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Bonce is British slang for a person's head or skull.

clue.text: Go last for ages

definitions.meaning: to go somewhere is to have one's proper place there, as in 'the cups go in that cupboard'
to take a long time or endure, read as two words

explanation.surface: A plea to go last and take your time.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that go somewhere have their right place there; split as two words, to be long is to take ages.

clue.text: Charity raising some awareness e.g. rallying

indicators.note: raising says the hidden letters are read backwards
some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A charity campaign raises awareness, for example by holding rallies.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'raising' means read upwards, so the hidden run is taken in reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Largesse is generous giving to others, especially of money, which is what charity means.

clue.text: Skill covered by 60s bird

indicators.note: covered by says the skill sits inside the next piece

parts.note: sixty seconds make a minute, MIN for short
art is skill, as in 'the art of conversation'

explanation.surface: A talent kept hidden by a 1960s pop idol, bird being slang for a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: '60s' suggests the decade, but it is 60 seconds.
explanation.definitionFit: The martin is a small bird of the swallow family, such as the house martin.

clue.text: They're not paid in rum at sea, unfortunately

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things gone wrong, so the letters are set in a new order

explanation.surface: Sailors grumble that they are paid not in money but in rum on board ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Amateurs take part for love rather than money, unlike professionals who receive pay.

clue.text: One writing Eric Blair's first and second works

indicators.note: works means the letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: first says to take the opening letter of Blair's

explanation.surface: A writer studies Eric Blair's earliest and next books.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric Blair was the real name of George Orwell, which makes 'works' look like his books.
explanation.definitionFit: A scribe is a person who writes, originally one who copied documents by hand.

clue.text: Are stylish clothes managed in turn during rebellious phase?

indicators.note: clothes is a verb here, the outer pieces dressing the inner one

parts.note: an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A
chic means stylish

indicators.note: in turn says the managed word is read backwards

parts.note: ran means managed, as in 'ran the shop'

explanation.surface: A teenager asks whether fashionable clothes were handled during a rebellious stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' looks like garments but is a verb meaning wraps; 'Are' is the metric unit of land area, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Anarchic means lawless and disorderly, the state of a youth in a period of rebelling against authority.

clue.text: He's seeing Pong entertaining priest

indicators.note: entertaining means holding within, as a host holds guests

parts.note: hum is British slang for a bad smell, as is pong
Eli is the priest in the Book of Samuel who raised Samuel

explanation.surface: A man is meeting a smelly person who is hosting a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' looks like a pronoun, but it is the chemical symbol of an element.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the chemical symbol of the light noble gas element number two.

clue.text: A Liverpool fan left female inside (one that was great)

parts.note: Liverpool FC play in red and their supporters are called Reds

explanation.surface: A Liverpool supporter left a woman inside, a once-great figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Liverpool is an English football club whose fans are nicknamed Reds.
explanation.definitionFit: King Alfred the Great ruled Wessex in the ninth century and is known by that epithet.

clue.text: Darts player in match gets 100

parts.note: to fit is to match, as in 'the key fits the lock'
a ton is a hundred, also darts slang for a score of 100

explanation.surface: A darts player scores a ton in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Darryl Fitton is an English professional darts player; ton is darts slang for a score of 100.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitton is the surname of the English professional darts player Darryl Fitton, named here by his sport.

clue.text: During Midsummer Eve, a light show

indicators.note: during says the answer lies within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: On Midsummer's Eve a light display takes place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'light show' reads as one phrase; the definition is only 'show', a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal something is to show it or disclose it to view.

clue.text: You're aroused, missing why Spaniard's ready for one

indicators.note: aroused means stirred up, so the remaining letters are rearranged
missing says that letter is dropped from the fodder

parts.note: why sounds like the letter Y, its usual crossword stand-in

explanation.surface: A seductive line about a Spaniard being ready for love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ready' is slang for cash, as in 'readies'.
explanation.definitionFit: The euro is the currency of Spain, so it is an example of the cash a Spaniard carries.

clue.text: Drink dedicated to engineer (no tips!)

indicators.note: to engineer is to construct or contrive, so the letters are rearranged
no tips says to drop the first and last letters of dedicated

explanation.surface: A drink is offered to an engineer who refuses gratuities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no tips' sounds like a refusal to pay gratuities; it trims the ends of 'dedicated'.
explanation.definitionFit: Iced tea is a cold beverage made from chilled tea, so a kind of drink.

clue.text: Donk's described by article — I think so, too

indicators.note: described by means drawn around, so the article encloses the setter

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
Donk is the setter, so from the setter's view he is me

explanation.surface: The setter is the subject of a newspaper article, and agrees with it.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by name or as 'me'; 'described' in its geometric sense means traced around.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying amen expresses agreement, as a congregation affirms a prayer.

clue.text: Demands help at last, when extended

indicators.note: when extended says that single letter is expanded into the full word it abbreviates, as in physics formulas where it stands for force per area
at last says to take only the final letter of the word help

explanation.surface: Someone insists that help has finally arrived now a deadline has been extended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at last' picks P, the last letter of 'help'; 'when extended' writes P out in full as the word it abbreviates in physics.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressure in the sense of heavy demands, as in the pressures of work, the stresses placed on someone.

clue.text: Thatcher's one for turning with "ore"?

indicators.note: turning means the letters are turned about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question whether Margaret Thatcher's supporter would turn when offered ore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thatcher' suggests the prime minister, but it is a tradesman who thatches roofs.
explanation.definitionFit: A thatcher roofs buildings with straw or reed, so is one kind of roofing tradesman.
